Cape Town Property & Holding Costs

How Are Cape Town Property Rates Calculated?The GV2025 Roll, the R620,000 Rebate and a Foreign Buyer's Rates Bill

2026.10.31 12 min read Scott Huang Offshore Property

In Cape Town, the purchase price is whatever you and the seller agree on. What you pay in property rates every year is not up to the two of you — it is decided by the number on the City of Cape Town's valuation roll. From 1 July 2026 the whole metro moved onto the GV2025 valuation roll: 970,000 properties revalued at market value as at 1 July 2025 and certified on 30 January 2026. In parallel, a Western Cape High Court judgment handed down on 30 April 2026 forced the City back to the table in May to rebuild the entire 2026/27 tariff structure — which is how the residential rebate climbed from R500,000 in the March draft to R620,000.

This article does one thing: it gets the first line of a foreign buyer's holding cost in Cape Town right — how property rates are calculated, what the roll change does to your bill, what the court ruling rewrote, and what is already moving in South Africa's 4 November local elections. Every figure carries its source and capture date. Cape Town rates and tariff structures are reset with the City's annual budget; this is information only, not investment or tax advice.

The short answer: Cape Town residential property rates are calculated as (municipal valuation − R620,000 rebate) × 0.7010%, and from 1 July 2026 the base is the GV2025 valuation roll. On a R6,000,000 Cape Town apartment that is about R37,714 a year, or roughly R3,143 a month (around NT$6,207); residential properties valued above R8,000,000 do not receive the R620,000 rebate. Property rates are only the first line of holding cost — in 2026 Cape Town water and electricity are rising far faster than rates themselves.

What Do Cape Town Property Rates Actually Tax — and How Does It Differ From Taiwan's House Tax?

It taxes ownership, not the transaction. Cape Town property rates are the annual local tax the City levies on immovable property. The base is the value recorded on the municipal valuation roll; the rate is set by the City's annual budget. It is a completely different instrument from transfer duty, which is a national tax collected by SARS and paid once at transfer. Property rates are paid every year for as long as you own in South Africa — including while the property stands empty.

ItemCape Town property ratesTaiwan house tax
Nature of the taxLocal tax, levied annuallyLocal tax, levied annually
Tax baseMarket value on the municipal valuation roll (GV2025 uses market value as at 1 July 2025)Assessed current value (announced-value system, persistently below market price)
Residential nominal rate0.7010% (R7.01 per R1,000 of taxable value)1.2% for owner-occupied homes
RebateResidential valuation at or below R8,000,000: first R620,000 excludedDepends on county-assessed value and owner-occupancy conditions
Who paysThe registered owner (the buyer), prorated daily from the date of transferThe property owner

⚠️ Do not stop at "1.2% is higher than 0.7010%". Taiwan's 1.2% is levied on an assessed value that sits far below market price, while Cape Town's 0.7010% is levied on the City's full market valuation. To compare the two, convert both into a share of market value — which is exactly why most Taiwanese buyers are taken aback by the size of a Cape Town rates bill the first time they see one.

The three things foreign buyers most often miss at transfer and afterwards

  • The seller must obtain a rates clearance certificate: before a South African transfer can be registered, the City must issue a certificate confirming the seller's municipal charges are settled. It is the seller's obligation, but a single delay pushes your registration date — and your remittance and renovation schedules are all pegged to that date in Cape Town.
  • The municipal account must be transferred into your name: once ownership is registered, the account has to move across to you. Skip it and the bill stays in the previous owner's name, leaving arrears, disconnections and deposit disputes as a three-way argument.
  • Rates are not the only fixed charge: water, electricity, sewerage and refuse each carry a fixed component plus a usage component, and sectional title or gated-estate property in Cape Town adds a community levy. Budgeting on rates alone badly understates the cost of holding property here.

Sources: City of Cape Town, "Rates and Tariffs Calculator" and "General and supplementary valuations" (GV2025 covers 970,000 properties, certified 30 January 2026, market value as at 1 July 2025); City of Cape Town 2026/27 adjusted budget announcement (27 May 2026: residential rate-in-the-rand 0.007010, rebate R620,000). (Source: City of Cape Town, 2026-05-27)

What Changed in the GV2025 Valuation Roll — and Why Are 2026 Cape Town Rates Different From Last Year?

Because the entire tax base was replaced. Cape Town runs a general valuation every few years, and GV2025 is the current roll: all 970,000 registered properties revalued to reflect market value as at 1 July 2025, certified on 30 January 2026, and used as the rates base from 1 July 2026. In other words, the Cape Town bill you receive after July 2026 and the amount you saw in 2025 are not calculated on the same base at all.

Four key GV2025 numbers

970,000 properties, certification on 30 January 2026, market-value date 1 July 2025, billing from 1 July 2026.

The City's own advice: run it twice

The City states explicitly that to assess the effect of a revaluation you must calculate twice — once on the GV2022 value and once on the GV2025 value.

That sentence is worth copying down, because it is simultaneously a method and a warning: "When assessing the impact of a change in valuation, the calculation must be done twice — once using the GV2022 value and once using the GV2025 value." The City itself concedes that a single new Cape Town bill does not reveal where the change came from. For a foreign buyer the practical meaning is blunt: the price you negotiate and the number on the municipal roll are two independent systems, and rates follow the roll, not your purchase price.

What if you missed the objection window? Use a supplementary valuation

The GV2025 objection window has closed. If, after buying in Cape Town, you believe the municipal value clearly misstates the property — wrong floor area, condition or use registration — the official route is to apply for a supplementary valuation, not to reopen the objection. This matters more for foreign buyers than for locals: you could not take part in the previous objection round, but you can request a supplementary valuation once you hold title in South Africa.

Sources: City of Cape Town, "General and supplementary valuations" (GV2025: 970,000 properties, certified 30 January 2026, market-value date 1 July 2025); City of Cape Town, "Current and upcoming valuations" (updated 2 September 2026: billed on GV2025 from 1 July 2026, supplementary valuation available to those who missed the objection window); City of Cape Town, "Rates and Tariffs Calculator" (the calculate-twice wording). (Source: City of Cape Town, 2026-09-02)

How Much Will a Foreign Buyer Pay? Five Cape Town Property Values Worked Through

The formula is one line: (municipal valuation − R620,000) × 0.007010 — divide by 12 for the monthly bill. The R620,000 rebate applies only where the residential valuation is R8,000,000 or below; above R8,000,000 the City's 27 May announcement states the rebate does not apply. The table below uses the adjusted 2026/27 residential rate for Cape Town:

Municipal valuation (ZAR)Taxable baseAnnual ratesMonthly ratesApprox. NT$ per year
R3,000,000R2,380,000R16,684approx. R1,390approx. NT$32,951
R6,000,000R5,380,000R37,714approx. R3,143approx. NT$74,485
R8,000,000R7,380,000R51,734approx. R4,311approx. NT$102,174
R12,000,000R12,000,000 (no rebate)R84,120approx. R7,010approx. NT$166,137
R20,000,000R20,000,000 (no rebate)R140,200approx. R11,683approx. NT$276,895

Conversion basis: ZAR 1 ≈ NT$1.975 (October 2026, indicative only — use the rate on the day you remit). The calculation covers property rates alone and excludes the fixed and usage charges for water, electricity, sewerage and refuse in Cape Town, and excludes the community levy.

Key insight: R8,000,000 is the break point in this table. A R6,000,000 Cape Town property carries an effective rate of about 0.629% because of the R620,000 rebate; a R20,000,000 property has no rebate and pays the full 0.701%. Same city, same tariff — the rebate trims the effective burden at the lower end by roughly a tenth, which is exactly why the City chose to raise the rebate rather than cut the rate when it reworked the budget after the court ruling.

Short-term letting and commercial use change your classification

Cape Town property rates are levied by property category: residential sits at a 1:1 ratio, while commercial and industrial is 1:2.41 (rate-in-the-rand 0.016910). Run a residential unit as long-stay short-term accommodation and the question is rarely "is it allowed" — it is "which category does the City put you in". Once the category changes in Cape Town, the annual bill does not rise by a few percentage points; it is multiplied by 2.41.

Sources: City of Cape Town, "Rates and Tariffs Calculator" (residential rate-in-the-rand 0.007010, residential rebate R620,000, including statutory relief); City of Cape Town 2026/27 adjusted budget announcement (27 May 2026: commercial and industrial rate-in-the-rand 0.016910, ratio 1:2.41; residential valuations below R8m qualify for the R620,000 rebate). (Source: City of Cape Town, 2026-05-27)

What Did the 30 April 2026 Court Ruling Change in Cape Town?

It changed who holds the power to spread fixed charges — and the City went back and rewrote its budget. On 30 April 2026 the Western Cape High Court ruled on the municipal tariff structure. In its 27 May announcement the City of Cape Town said that giving effect to the judgment "compelled the City to make several material amendments" to the rates and tariff structure submitted in March 2026/27. At the core of the ruling is a limit on the City's practice of cross-subsidising fixed charges through property value bands.

ItemBefore the ruling (March submission)After the ruling (May revision)
Residential rates rebateR500,000R620,000 (including statutory relief)
Residential rate-in-the-rand0.0064280.007010
Movement in residential rates−10.2%−2.09%
Commercial / industrial rate-in-the-rand0.015106 (ratio 1:2.35)0.016910 (ratio 1:2.41)
Fixed water and sewerage chargesBy property value bandBack to water-meter diameter

What the ruling means for a foreign buyer depends on your price bracket: Cape Town properties valued below R2,800,000 pay more for fixed water and sewerage, while higher-value properties pay less, because fixed charges are no longer tied to property value. At the same time the City lifted the valuation ceiling for the R620,000 rebate from R7,000,000 to R8,000,000, so lower- and mid-priced households absorb the fixed-charge increase through a larger rebate.

No appeal, and the ruling applies from 1 July 2026

The City confirmed it will not appeal the judgment, and stated that it operates prospectively, from 1 July 2026; charges already levied in 2025/26 are not backdated. Cape Town has also opened discussions with National Treasury and Cogta, the department of cooperative governance, on alternative instruments that would preserve cross-subsidisation inside the framework of the ruling. This is the thread to watch in South Africa over the next few years — it decides whether fixed charges get rewritten a second time.

Sources: City of Cape Town media release, "City expands rates relief to shield households from court ruling impact" (27 May 2026: post-judgment revision, R620,000 rebate, rate-in-the-rand comparison table, no appeal, effect from 1 July 2026, discussions with National Treasury and Cogta); City of Cape Town, "Rates and Tariffs Calculator" (states that the 30 April 2026 Western Cape High Court judgment drove the tariff restructure). (Source: City of Cape Town, 2026-05-27)

Western Cape Inflation Is 5.5% — Is It Rising Faster Than Your Cape Town Property Rates?

Far faster — and it is not rates that is moving. In September 2026 South African headline CPI rose 4.5% year on year, but the Western Cape ran at 5.5%, a full percentage point above the national figure, with a 0.5% monthly rise against 0.4% nationally. Broken down, what is really eating into the cost of holding Cape Town property is water and electricity rather than property rates: water and miscellaneous services +10.1% year on year, electricity +6.8%, actual residential rent +5.9% and insurance +6.3%.

Item (September 2026, year on year)Western CapeWhat it means for holding cost
Headline CPI5.5%A full point above the national 4.5%
Water and miscellaneous services+10.1%Rising at more than ten times the pace of rates, yet the most commonly omitted line in Cape Town budgets
Electricity+6.8%Felt hardest in properties with air conditioning and pool heating
Actual residential rent+5.9%Supports gross rental yield and sets the basis for lease reviews
Insurance+6.3%A fixed cost foreign buyers routinely overlook in South Africa
Food+3.1%Below the national average — the pressure is not at the dinner table

The City of Cape Town's three-year projections are blunter still: between 2025/26 and 2028/29 water may rise cumulatively by 36% and electricity by 24% (the actual impact varies with household usage and tariff category). That leads to one conclusion: assessing holding cost as "rates as a percentage of price" systematically understates it in Cape Town. The sound method is to put rates, water, electricity, insurance and the community levy into a single annual cash flow, then work back to the yield you actually require.

Key insight: rents up 5.9%, utilities up 6.8% to 10.1% — subtract the two and the number is negative. That is not a verdict that Cape Town yields are collapsing; it is a reminder that the gap between gross yield (market reference range around 9.49%) and net yield widened in 2026 because of utility costs. Net yield has to be recalculated, not carried over from last year's assumption.

Sources: StatsSA CPI for September 2026 (published 21 October 2026); The South African, "The Western Cape leads South Africa in inflation" (24 October 2026: Western Cape 5.5%, water and miscellaneous +10.1%, electricity +6.8%, actual rent +5.9%, insurance +6.3%, food +3.1%); Cape Argus / IOL, "Cost of Cape Town water and electricity to skyrocket over the next three years" (23 October 2026: water +36%, electricity +24% from 2025/26 to 2028/29). (Source: StatsSA, 2026-10-21)

After the 4 November Elections, What Is Already in Motion in Cape Town?

Three things are already running, and none of them waits for the election result. South Africa votes in local elections on 4 November 2026, and Cape Town — a metro the governing party has held for years — has housing and living costs as live campaign issues. But what matters to a foreign owner is not who wins; it is the tariff variables already inside statutory process, because their timetables do not reset on election night.

1

Already in force: the 30 April 2026 judgment and the tariff structure from 1 July

The judgment takes effect from 1 July 2026 and the City is not appealing. Fixed water and sewerage charges calculated on water-meter diameter are therefore the standing system in Cape Town, and an election result does not reverse them.

2

Already through council: supplementary public participation on the 2026/27 adjusted budget

The City opened supplementary public participation on the budget revision from 27 May to 10 June and adopted it before the new financial year on 1 July. That process is complete, but the tariff ratios — residential 1:1, commercial 1:2.41 — are renegotiated inside every annual budget in Cape Town.

3

Already under discussion: an alternative to cross-subsidisation with National Treasury and Cogta

The ruling rejected cross-subsidisation delivered through property value bands, and Cape Town has started talks with National Treasury and the department of cooperative governance on replacement instruments. This is the line that decides whether fixed charges are rewritten again in South Africa, and it turns on national departments rather than the ballot.

After the vote, watch two actions — not the parties

First, whether the new council adjusts the tariff ratio in the 2027/28 budget — that decides whether the commercial-to-residential ratio climbs above 1:2.41. Second, whether Cape Town takes its alternative cross-subsidisation model to national departments as legislation or guidance — that decides whether the fixed-charge formula gets rewritten once more. Both land directly on your annual municipal bill, and both are visible in public documents. No political forecasting required.

Sources: Reuters, "Battleground metros to watch in South Africa's municipal elections" (26 October 2026: polling day 4 November 2026); City of Cape Town media release (27 May 2026: supplementary public participation 27 May to 10 June, adoption before 1 July, discussions with National Treasury and Cogta); City of Cape Town, "General and supplementary valuations" (GV2025 objection period and the supplementary valuation route). (Source: Reuters, 2026-10-26)

FAQ

What annual holding taxes does a foreign buyer pay on Cape Town property?

Three main lines: property rates (calculated on the GV2025 municipal valuation and the City's rate-in-the-rand), utilities (water, electricity, sewerage and refuse, each with a fixed charge plus a usage charge), and the community levy on sectional title or gated-estate property. Insurance and security are usually billed separately. Property rates is the only one of the three based on the value of the property.

Does the R620,000 rebate apply to every Cape Town property owner?

No. Under the City of Cape Town's 27 May 2026 announcement, residential property valued at R8,000,000 or below excludes the first R620,000 from the taxable value; residential property above R8,000,000 does not receive the rebate. What actually applies is determined by the City's rates policy for that financial year and by your own bill.

Is my Cape Town property rates bill based on the price I paid?

No. Property rates are calculated on the value in the municipal valuation roll (GV2025), a separate system from your purchase price. Paying above the municipal value is common, and paying below it also happens; a mismatch does not automatically adjust your bill. If the recorded area, condition or use is wrong, the route is a supplementary valuation.

What are the monthly property rates on a R6,000,000 Cape Town apartment?

Using the 2026/27 residential rate, about R3,143 a month (R37,714 a year), assuming the municipal valuation is R6,000,000 and the R620,000 rebate applies — roughly NT$6,207 a month. That figure covers property rates only, not water, electricity or the community levy. It is a market-reference calculation, not a quote from the City.

I think the City's valuation of my property is too high. Can I still object?

The GV2025 objection window has closed. The official route now is to apply for a supplementary valuation to have the property reassessed. Where the error comes from recorded floor area, condition or use, a supplementary valuation is the main remedy; gather your plans and current-condition evidence after taking transfer in Cape Town, then apply.

Does short-term letting change the property rates on a Cape Town home?

Yes. Property rates are levied by property category, with residential at a 1:1 ratio and commercial and industrial at 1:2.41 after the 2026/27 adjustment. Whether long-run short-stay letting counts as commercial use depends on the City's rates policy and the facts of the case, so confirm the category before you commit rather than after the bill arrives.

Why Handle This Through Crestline Advisory?

In Cape Town, what goes wrong with municipal rates and the valuation roll is almost never the "rate" itself — it is the property data and the timing of the procedure. When the recorded area, use or condition on the roll differs from the property on the ground, the bill simply keeps being wrong.

The three points where people most often get stuck

  • No GV2025 check before transfer: the price is agreed, and only then does it emerge that the municipal valuation sits well above expectation, adding a whole line to the annual rates bill. Checking the roll costs nothing — most overseas buyers simply do not know it has to be checked, or which tool to check it with.
  • The seller's rates clearance certificate is not in place: no South African transfer can be registered without the City's clearance certificate. If the seller owes money or the paperwork is incomplete, the registration date slips day by day — and the remittance, renovation and letting schedules queued behind it in Cape Town all move with it.
  • The municipal account is never transferred: once title is registered, the account must move into the buyer's name. Skip it and the bill stays with the previous owner, and arrears, disconnections and deposit disputes later turn into a three-way argument.

Working through our partner Crestline Advisory (on-the-ground execution in South Africa), these are confirmed before anyone acts: the GV2025 valuation and recent bills are pulled and modelled into a holding-cost estimate before transfer, the progress of the seller's rates clearance application is confirmed, the municipal account transfer and deposit settlement are handled after registration in Cape Town, and where relevant a supplementary valuation is assessed.
